title: The First Poet
tagline: He heard a bird cry for its slain mate — and composed the world's first Sanskrit verse.

scenes.text: Ancient India, perhaps 500 BCE. A hermit named Valmiki walks in the forest and witnesses something that stops him cold: a hunter's arrow strikes down a male krauncha bird just as it mates with its partner. The surviving bird screams in grief. And from that scream, something new is born.

scenes.speaker: Valmiki
scenes.text: The words came out as a curse against the hunter — but they fell into a rhythm I had never spoken before. Equal syllables, balanced cadence, a pattern that carried emotion like a vessel carries water. I had not composed this. It had composed itself from grief. I called it a shloka.

params.title: Equal Syllables
params.intro: Valmiki's verse fell into four balanced quarters. Restore the square so every row, column and both long diagonals share one sum.
params.fact: Sanskrit metres are counted in syllables, light and heavy, not in stresses. Pingala's Chandahshastra, a few centuries BCE, set out every pattern of light and heavy syllables — an early cousin of binary counting.

challenge.instruction: The words came out in a rhythm Valmiki had never spoken: four quarters, equal syllables, every part in balance. Make every line of the square balance the same way.
challenge.fact: Tradition calls Valmiki the Adi Kavi, the first poet, and his Ramayana the Adi Kavya, the first poem of Sanskrit literature. The epic opens with the story of how he came to poetry, before it tells a single deed of Rama.

scenes.text: The god Brahma appeared to Valmiki and commanded him to use this new form to tell the story of Rama — a prince, an exile, a war, a rescue, a homecoming. The result was the Ramayana: 24,000 verses, seven books, and one of the central stories of human civilization.

scenes.speaker: Brahma
scenes.text: Valmiki, compose the tale of Rama in the verse form born from your grief. As long as mountains stand and rivers flow, so long will the Ramayana be told.

challenge.instruction: Brahma has given Valmiki the story of Rama, and it begins with exile. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana have left Ayodhya; take Guha's boat across the Ganga.
challenge.fact: The Ramayana centers on Prince Rama of Ayodhya — his exile with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana, Sita's abduction by the demon king Ravana, and Rama's journey to rescue her with the help of Hanuman and an army of monkeys. It remains one of Asia's most beloved epics.

scenes.speaker: Valmiki
scenes.text: I am called Adi Kavi — the First Poet — not because no one spoke in rhythm before me, but because I was the first to understand what poetry is for. It is not ornament. It is not entertainment. Poetry is how the soul speaks when ordinary language is too small for what must be said.

challenge.instruction: Valmiki's verses follow Rama south. Lead the exiles from Chitrakuta to Panchavati, where Sita is taken, then to Kishkindha and the shore of the southern sea.
challenge.fact: The Ramayana's themes — the duty of a prince, the devotion of a wife, the loyalty of a friend — have resonated across Asia for 2,500 years. The epic has more than 300 known versions across South and Southeast Asia, each reflecting the values of its culture.

scenes.text: The Ramayana has been told, retold, translated, dramatized, and danced in every language and culture of South and Southeast Asia for 2,500 years. Its characters — Rama's righteousness, Sita's faithfulness, Hanuman's devotion, Ravana's pride — became archetypes for human virtue and human failing.

challenge.instruction: Every telling of the Ramayana goes back to one riverbank. Put the moment in order — the river, the two birds, the hunter's arrow and the verse that grief made.
challenge.fact: The shloka metre — the pattern Valmiki invented in that moment of grief — became the dominant verse form of Sanskrit epic poetry. The Mahabharata, the Puranas, and thousands of religious texts all use the same metre that Valmiki created spontaneously, in sorrow, beside a river.

scenes.speaker: Valmiki
scenes.text: I was a forest hermit. I had no army, no kingdom, no gold. But I had words arranged in a form that could carry a story across centuries. Rama will be remembered long after every king of his era is forgotten. The pen that writes the poem outlasts the sword that builds the empire.

challenge.instruction: The war that ends the tale: Rama faces Ravana's champions at Lanka. Choose the right weapon for each foe — the poem that tells it will outlast every king.
challenge.fact: The Ramayana has influenced cultures across Southeast Asia for over a thousand years. Thailand has the Ramakien, Indonesia has the Kakawin Ramayana, and Cambodia's Reamker is performed at the royal court. Puppetry and dance forms based on the Ramayana are UNESCO-listed cultural traditions in Malaysia, Thailand, and Myanmar.

scenes.speaker: Valmiki
scenes.text: Zeno of Elea and Mahavira hold Rome together, and a follower stands with them. One card alone will not move them. Bring Mani with me, add both followers, and strike twice.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 2 · Strength in Numbers. Over two turns stack Valmiki, Mani and both followers at Rome, then win two attacks against the rival side.
challenge.fact: An attack compares whole sides at a location, not single cards. Two Great People and two followers in the same stat outweigh a rival who arrived first, and each win sends one rival card back to its owner's hand.
